# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content.content: # Reusable workflow: builds a repo's privacy policy into a one-page GitHub # Pages site and deploys it at the fixed permalink /privacy/ — # https://.github.io//privacy/ # The Jekyll `permalink` pins that public path independent of where PRIVACY.md # lives in the repo (move the file → only the input below changes, never the # URL). The page body is the caller's PRIVACY.md verbatim — the single source # of truth, no duplicated copy. # # Deliberately NOT Chrome-specific (hence the unprefixed name): any publish # standard whose store listing needs a live privacy-policy URL deploys through # it. workflow_call ONLY — it never runs in Claudinite itself. # Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism

How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the tick's post-tick drain,
   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its prework, and either
   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.

The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.

There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
than by replaying a ledger.

## What the checks guard

- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored tick — no logic of its own
  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Recurring work that had its own cron'd workflow
  becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted — its steps move into the
  task's worker. Don't keep it as a dispatch-only workflow for the task to fire:
  that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a workflow whose only
  caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run *as an Action*
  for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, say — is the
  exception, and even then the task owns the schedule.) Off-band or multiple
  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
  safety, or manual runs.

- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly | manual`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
  tick and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the work
  item — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
  the next entry.

- **A task's code reads only the environment prework is handed.** Prework runs as
  a subprocess with a fixed set of `CLAUDINITE_*` variables — `REPO_ROOT`, `REPO`,
  `DEFAULT_BRANCH`, `ITEM`, `PACK`, `TASK`, `CONTEXT`, `REQUEST_AGENT` — and
  `task-prework-env` (blocking) rejects a read of anything else. A variable nobody
  sets is `undefined`, the parse of it yields empty, and the run goes green having
  quietly done something other than what it was asked: that is how three fleet
  tasks kept taking their parameters through a channel the queue had stopped
  setting, leaving a fleet-wide sweep unable to be scoped or dry-run. **Operator
  parameters ride the item's Context** (`CLAUDINITE_CONTEXT`, one line per bullet),
  which is the only channel a task may take them from.

- **Session scope is retired, and `session_scope` is now inert** (owner ruling,
  2026-08-09; the field's last reader went with the slot scheduler). Reach is a
  property of **which endpoint the hand-off calls** — `invocation_endpoint`, below

content.text:
Three reasons, and they're all in the file itself ([`deploy-privacy-page.yml`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/.github/workflows/deploy-privacy-page.yml)):

**1. It isn't scheduled work — there's no cron to own.** The workflow is `workflow_call` only. Its trigger is "a store publish just shipped": it's a leg of [`chrome-extension-publish-store.yml`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/.github/workflows/chrome-extension-publish-store.yml) (line 120). The rule in [`core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) that says "recurring work that had its own cron'd workflow becomes a task, and that workflow is deleted" is about *cron'd* work. This has no cron. Converting it to a task would mean inventing a schedule for something that should fire on an event, and then having a periodic agent session ask "did anything publish?" instead of the publish just calling it.

**2. A task literally cannot do the deploy.** Pages deployment needs `id-token: write` to mint an OIDC token that `actions/deploy-pages@v4` exchanges, plus the `github-pages` environment with its branch policy. Those exist only inside an Actions run — an agent session holds `GITHUB_TOKEN`, not an OIDC identity for the Pages environment. This is exactly the exception the contract names: *"A workflow that must run as an Action for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, say — is the exception, and even then the task owns the schedule."* Here there's no schedule for the task to own either, so nothing is left for it.

**3. The work is deterministic.** `cat PRIVACY.md` into a front-mattered file, jekyll-build, upload. There is no judgment in it. Spending an opus session per deploy on a step with one correct output buys non-determinism and cost, not value.

Note the same file already reaches for Claudinite where Claudinite is the right tool: the `report-failure` job files a tracking issue, because *that* part — noticing an unattended red run and converging it into something a human sees — is what the task/queue machinery is for.

So the split holds: **Actions execute the privileged, deterministic act; Claudinite owns the schedule, the judgment and the follow-up.** The only thing that would change my answer is if you wanted the page refreshed on a cadence independent of publishes (e.g. nightly re-deploy if `PRIVACY.md` drifted) — then a task should own that schedule and `wake` a dispatch, but the deploy leg would still be an Action for reason 2.

> ✅ All done — no changes made; this was a question. Answered from the workflow file and the scheduled-tasks contract.

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. - adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. - pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

input.title: Task phase language: rename `prework` → `code_work`, and stop framing tasks as scheduled-only
input.body:
Two owner corrections to the task-execution vocabulary, raised in session.

## 1. Tasks are not only for scheduled events

The corpus repeatedly frames a task as *recurring/scheduled* work. It isn't: `frequency: 'manual'` is a first-class non-cadence, tasks are woken by event and by force, and a "nightly release only if there were pack updates" is an event-gated task, not a cadence. Amend the places that assert or imply the scheduled-only framing.

## 2. `prework` is the wrong name for the code phase

A task's execution is two phases. The first runs deterministic code in the executor (an Actions run); the second runs an agent. Some tasks use only the first. Calling it *pre*work frames it as secondary to, and preparation for, the agent — it isn't; it just happens to run first.

Rename to **code-work** vs **agentic-work**:

- declaration fields `prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`
- engine modules, check id, symbols, tests, prose

This repeats the shape of the 2026-08-06 rename (`agent_preprocessing` → `prework`), which failed to fix the framing — the new name kept the agent as the reference point. Same mechanism as that one: legacy names accepted and normalized at load, a migration record, and the `task-declaration-shape` finding as the durable driver for member local packs.

## Out of scope

The prior migration record (`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/`) is a historical record and keeps its own wording.

content.text: Now the mechanical sweep. Writing a precise replacement script:

input.command:
cat > /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Claudinite/fe74455a-3890-5eb7-be07-82c69e7e3321/scratchpad/rename.py <<'PY'
import re, subprocess, sys, os

files = subprocess.run(['git','ls-files'],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.split()

# Excluded: the 2026-08-06 migration record states a historical fact about a
# rename that happened; and generated files come from their generators.
def excluded(p):
    if p.startswith('engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/'): return True
    if 'GENERATED' in p: return True
    return False

# Ordered, longest-first. `prework-rename` (the prior migration's id) and
# `agent_preprocessing` (its legacy input) are deliberately untouched.
COMMON = [
    (r'prework-rename', 'prework-rename'),          # sentinel: protected below
    (r'prework_timeout', 'code_work_timeout'),
    (r'runTaskPrework', 'runTaskCodeWork'),
    (r'runPrework', 'runCodeWork'),
    (r'preworkMinutes', 'codeWorkMinutes'),
    (r'preworkFailure', 'codeWorkFailure'),
    (r'preworkFails', 'codeWorkFails'),
    (r'preworkRunner', 'codeWorkRunner'),
    (r'preworkEnv', 'codeWorkEnv'),
    (r'legacyPrework', 'legacyCodeWork'),
    (r'hasPrework', 'hasCodeWork'),
    (r'taskPreworkEnv', 'taskCodeWorkEnv'),
    (r'task-prework-env', 'task-code-work-env'),
    (r'task-prework', 'task-code-work'),
    (r'prework-run', 'code-work-run'),
    (r'fixture-prework', 'fixture-code-work'),
    (r'prework\.mjs', 'code-work.mjs'),
    (r'PREWORK', 'CODE-WORK'),
]

PROTECT = 'prework-rename'
TOKEN = '\x00PROTECTED\x00'

changed = []
for p in files:
    if excluded(p): continue
    try:
        s = open(p, encoding='utf-8').read()
    except (UnicodeDecodeError, IsADirectoryError):
        continue
    if 'prework' not in s.lower(): continue
    orig = s
    s = s.replace(PROTECT, TOKEN)
    for pat, rep in COMMON[1:]:
        s = re.sub(pat, rep, s)
    # Bare `prework` / `Prework`: the declaration FIELD in code and in
    # backticks; the concept spelled code-work in running prose.
    if p.endswith('.md'):
        s = re.sub(r'`prework`', '`code_work`', s)
        s = re.sub(r'"prework"', '"code_work"', s)
        s = re.sub(r'\bprework\b', 'code-work', s)
        s = re.sub(r'\bPrework\b', 'Code-work', s)
    else:
        s = re.sub(r'\bprework\b', 'code_work', s)
        s = re.sub(r'\bPrework\b', 'Code-work', s)
    s = s.replace(TOKEN, PROTECT)
    if s != orig:
        open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
        changed.append(p)

print(f'{len(changed)} files rewritten')
PY

    Shim the engine paths fielded pack copies still import (#1006)

    task-declaration-shape.mjs imports engine/scheduler/slots.mjs.
    
    The engine lane and the pack lane deliver in separate PRs on separate
    cycles and pack delivery is version-gated per pack, so every member spends
    a window holding the new engine beside an old pack. Nothing closes that
    window. A packs/ file importing an engine/ module is therefore a stale
    caller of an instantly-current engine — the same asymmetry updates/* already
    carries, one lane over.
    
    It is worse than a broken task: a pack that fails to load fails the mount's
    self-test, so the converge refuses to land at all and the member cannot

content.content:
# Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism

How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
...
  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored tick — no logic of its own
  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Recurring work that had its own cron'd workflow
  becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted — its steps move into the
  task's worker. Don't keep it as a dispatch-only workflow for the task to fire:
  that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a workflow whose only
  caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run *as an Action*
  for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, say — is the
  exception, and even then the task owns the schedule.) Off-band or multiple
  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
  safety, or manual runs.

This shapes the "hard-code the deterministic parts" boundary above into concrete files, governed by four rules:
packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md:49:- **Give each unattended recurring routine its own standing tracking issue as a self-improvement log, titled exactly `Claudinite tracker: <Name>`.** Find it by that **exact title string, never a fuzzy or partial match** and never a bare number (a number can dangle, and a partial match risks landing on the wrong issue). Log every run that produces a change there — as a **dated comment**, not a sub-issue — so the routine's output accumulates in one reviewable feed, making it easy to audit what it did over time and to tell when the routine itself needs tuning. One issue per routine, not a shared parent. **Create it already closed** if it doesn't exist yet — that is **two calls**, because issue creation always lands the issue open and a `state: closed` argument on the create call is silently ignored: create it, then close it with a follow-up update. And **never open, close, or reopen it again afterward** — its state carries no meaning here (it's a log, not a work item), so every run leaves the state exactly as found and only ever appends. When the routine reports a **current state** rather than a stream of discrete changes (a branch/PR report, a status roll-up), keep that state in the issue **body**, rewritten each run so the newest snapshot is at the top, and use the dated comments as the per-run trail — the reader sees today's picture first, not the oldest one. (Worked examples: `docs/claude/auto-lessons.md` #365, `docs/claude/auto-fallback-coverage.md` #366, `docs/claude/auto-branch-report.md` #399.) **Read that log before authoring anything the routine may have attempted before** — each run re-derives its candidates independently from the same sources, so runs converge on the same item and re-hit the same rejection; make reading the log a precondition of authoring, not a formatting step at the end. **Read the open PRs touching the same paths too, for the same reason**: where the routine's output is review-gated, a finished run's work sits unmerged and the next run — reading only the default branch — cannot see it, so it redoes the work and throws the earlier PR's copy away. An open PR is work already done; when one already answers the question, say so on it and get it reviewed rather than answering it twice.

input.body:
Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |
| run-record wire word | `code-work`, kebab because the line format's charset (`[a-z-]+`) never admitted an underscore. `preprocess` and `prework` in a job log still parse |
| usage aggregate | its counter keys are those same words and it holds rows written under the old ones. The decode renames them; without that the next encode wrote the count as `null` |
| `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` | kept as a re-export shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and the engine and pack lanes deliver separately (#1004, #1006) |

## Verification

- Full suite: **2097 pass, 0 fail** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking, 57 advisory** — byte-identical to the same run stashed against `main`, so no finding is new.
- `engine/selftest.mjs`: 5 probes passed.
- **See-it-fail on both new guards.** Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously). Disabling the counter rename writes the historical count as `[3,null,1,0,0]`; two new tests in `usage-format.test.mjs` pin it, including a row carrying both spellings at once.

## Out of scope

`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/` keeps its own wording — it states what that rename did, which has not changed. Its id is likewise still spelled `prework-rename` wherever it is referenced.

| unmodeled element | what the real world does | what defends the design there |
|---|---|---|
| **Cron delivery** | `schedule:` is a request to queue: fires land minutes-to-tens-of-minutes late, are silently dropped under load, and GitHub disables schedules after 60 days of repo inactivity ([github-actions-scheduling](../../../.claude/skills/github-actions-scheduling/SKILL.md)) | late/dropped fires ARE modeled abstractly (`dropTicks`/`tickAt` — S4, S5); every rule derives due-ness from durable state, never from "the cron fired"; the 60-day disable is inherited risk, mitigated as today (repo activity from the mechanism's own writes) |
| **Actions start latency** | a queued workflow may wait minutes before running; the drain is not really at tick+40s | nothing depends on start latency; all deadlines (leashes, staleness) are hours against minutes of jitter |
| **Tick serialization** | two ticks racing is prevented by the workflow `concurrency` group, an Actions feature the sim assumes rather than models | S6 models the *guards* under a duplicated fire; the group is platform config, verified in the migration burst (B1) |

# Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism

How a repo's own Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

**A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is.** A task is a
unit of the repo's own work with a precondition, a code-work phase and optionally an
agentic-work phase; `frequency` says only how often the queue offers to run it, and
`manual` — no cadence at all — is a first-class value. Work that fires on an event,
on a condition, or on a force is a task in exactly the same sense as work that fires
nightly, and reads the same contract. Anything reachable from the executor belongs
here rather than in a workflow of its own; see the cron rule below for the narrow
case that genuinely cannot be.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics

content.text:
CI is still running on the final commit; the background timer and PR subscription will bring me back to it. Here's where things stand.

**You were right on all three, and my original answer was wrong in a way worth naming:** I reasoned from the vocabulary the docs happened to use rather than from the mechanism. "Tasks are scheduled work" and "prework is preparation for the agent" are both things the corpus *says*, and I repeated them as if they were things the system *does*.

## What landed — [#1013](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1013), closes [#1012](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1012)

**Item 1 — scheduled-only framing.** [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) now says a cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is. The cron rule previously offered the task conversion only to work that *already had a cron* — which is precisely what made event-driven work read as out of scope — and now covers work with no cadence at all. The Actions-only exception is narrowed from "the whole job" to "the step that needs the Action's own privileges." I retitled the doc but left its filename: `scheduled-tasks.md` has 28 references across 18 files, several inside check `fix` strings members read, so that rename is its own change.

**Item 2 — `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work.`** 139 files. The interesting part is that this rename has now happened twice: `agent_preprocessing` → `prework` in August tried to fix exactly this framing and didn't, because it kept the agent as the implicit reference point. Five compatibility surfaces carry both old spellings, and two of them were real bugs I had to find rather than transcribe:

- The run-record **wire word** is `code-work`, kebab — the line format's regex is `[a-z-]+` and never accepted an underscore, so `code_work` silently stopped parsing.
- The **usage aggregate** stores those same words as counter keys and holds rows written under the old ones. Its self-describing header decoded them fine; the next *encode* wrote the count as `null`. I proved that (`[3,null,1,0,0]`) before fixing it, and pinned it with tests including a row carrying both spellings.

Also kept `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` as a shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and per #1004/#1006 a vanished engine module fails the mount self-test and wedges the converge. I confirmed the shim is load-bearing by deleting it and watching `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` go red. That test needed `--depth=200` to mean anything; on this shallow clone it self-guards and would have passed vacuously.

**Verification:** 2097 tests pass; `check_the_world` is byte-identical to `main` (0 blocking, 57 advisory). First CI push failed on two work-scope checks my world-scope local run couldn't see — six missing pack version bumps, and a pre-existing dangling link in the sim README that pointed at the per-session flat `.claude/skills/` mount. Both fixed and re-verified with CI's own `ci-work-scope.mjs` locally.

**One thing I did not do:** the 2026-08-06 migration record keeps its wording and its `prework-rename` id — it states what that rename did, which hasn't changed.

On the deployment job: you're right that "no partial retries" and "no visibility into ongoing tasks" are the real axes, and I'd add that the executor's code-work phase already *is* an Actions run, which dissolves my "a task can't hold the OIDC identity" argument — the code-work subprocess runs in the same place `deploy-pages` would. Happy to pick that up when you are.

> ⚠️ Still open: CI on [#1013](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1013) is still in progress on the final commit (`e2ba341`) — two earlier commits' worth of failures are fixed and re-verified locally, but I haven't yet seen this run go green. I'm subscribed and will drive it to green without further prompting. Separately unaddressed by choice: renaming `scheduled-tasks.md` itself, and returning to the GitHub Pages deployment question.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

{"number":1013,"title":"Rename the code phase to code-work, and stop calling tasks scheduled-only","body":"Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

{"number":1013,"title":"Rename the code phase to code-work, and stop calling tasks scheduled-only","body":"Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |
| run-record wire word | `code-work`, kebab because the line format's charset (`[a-z-]+`) never admitted an underscore. `preprocess` and `prework` in a job log still parse |
| usage aggregate | its counter keys are those same words and it holds rows written under the old ones. The decode renames them; without that the next encode wrote the count as `null` |
| `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` | kept as a re-export shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and the engine and pack lanes deliver separately (#1004, #1006) |

## Verification

- Full suite: **2097 pass, 0 fail** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking, 57 advisory** — byte-identical to the same run stashed against `main`, so no finding is new.
- `engine/selftest.mjs`: 5 probes passed.
- **See-it-fail on both new guards.** Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously). Disabling the counter rename writes the historical count as `[3,null,1,0,0]`; two new tests in `usage-format.test.mjs` pin it, including a row carrying both spellings at once.

## Out of scope

`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/` keeps its own wording — it states what that rename did, which has not changed. Its id is likewise still spelled `prework-rename` wherever it is referenced.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. {"number":1013,"title":"Rename the code phase to code-work, and stop calling tasks scheduled-only","body":"Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |
| run-record wire word | `code-work`, kebab because the line format's charset (`[a-z-]+`) never admitted an underscore. `preprocess` and `prework` in a job log still parse |
| usage aggregate | its counter keys are those same words and it holds rows written under the old ones. The decode renames them; without that the next encode wrote the count as `null` |
| `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` | kept as a re-export shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and the engine and pack lanes deliver separately (#1004, #1006) |

## Verification

- Full suite: **2097 pass, 0 fail** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking, 57 advisory** — byte-identical to the same run stashed against `main`, so no finding is new.
- `engine/selftest.mjs`: 5 probes passed.
- **See-it-fail on both new guards.** Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously). Disabling the counter rename writes the historical count as `[3,null,1,0,0]`; two new tests in `usage-format.test.mjs` pin it, including a row carrying both spellings at once.

## Out of scope

`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/` keeps its own wording — it states what that rename did, which has not changed. Its id is likewise still spelled `prework-rename` wherever it is referenced.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. {"number":1013,"title":"Rename the code phase to code-work, and stop calling tasks scheduled-only","body":"Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |
| run-record wire word | `code-work`, kebab because the line format's charset (`[a-z-]+`) never admitted an underscore. `preprocess` and `prework` in a job log still parse |
| usage aggregate | its counter keys are those same words and it holds rows written under the old ones. The decode renames them; without that the next encode wrote the count as `null` |
| `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` | kept as a re-export shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and the engine and pack lanes deliver separately (#1004, #1006) |

## Verification

- Full suite: **2097 pass, 0 fail** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking, 57 advisory** — byte-identical to the same run stashed against `main`, so no finding is new.
- `engine/selftest.mjs`: 5 probes passed.
- **See-it-fail on both new guards.** Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously). Disabling the counter rename writes the historical count as `[3,null,1,0,0]`; two new tests in `usage-format.test.mjs` pin it, including a row carrying both spellings at once.

## Out of scope

`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/` keeps its own wording — it states what that rename did, which has not changed. Its id is likewise still spelled `prework-rename` wherever it is referenced.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
